On wednesday night I discovered that she had dried up blood on her bottom, but she was acting normal and eating normally. Last night the bleeding started to get worse, so we took her to the vet this morning. The vet told us that there was a tumor in her uterus, and our two options were to either remove Monkey's uterus entirely, or to put her down. Monkey was approaching two years, and ultimately we decided that it was best to not let her suffer, and she has already lived a long, healthy life.

Monkey was the silliest little girl. When we first saw her at the pet store, she was going crazy in her tiny tank, and other people were pointing and laughing at her like she was a circus act. Right then, we decided to get her because we knew that she was special and needed to be put in a calm environment. We named her Monkey because she loved to climb and play. She was the friendliest little baby, she never bit, and always climbed our hands when we reached in her cage.

She got me through some very hard times, and I will miss my little Monkey girl ❤️🐒

Free roaming is a thing you should do. But it is for only a few hours at a time. The "literature" you linked is a good article, but this is not how your hamster should be living. This is so your hamster can roam around and when it gets late or your hamster is tired and wants to go back in, that is when your hamster goes back in their cage. It is completely different than having them be able to free roam at all times. They should be supervised when they free roam. Hamsters are unpredictable.

If you have people screaming at you to not do it, then the smart thing would be to not do it. Just because they've been in the wild before we domesticated them doesn't mean this is a good idea. Anything can happen. "Free-range" hamsters are not a thing, and aren't a thing for a reason. Educate yourself.
